What they are
A response paper is a short piece of thinking, not summary: take the week’s required readings and do something with them — challenge an argument, apply it to a case the author didn’t use, put two readings into conflict, or connect the reading to something happening now.
The test: could someone who has done the reading learn something from your response? Restating the argument fails that test; arguing with it passes.

title: POU33201 — Reading response papers
section: What a good one probably looks like
text:
What a good one probably looks like

Leads with your claim, not the author’s.
Uses the reading precisely — one concept or finding, named.
Brings a case or comparison the reading didn’t use.
Ends with a genuine question for the room.

You do not need sources beyond the week’s readings, and there is no bibliography. Cite by author and page where you are using something specific.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Module description
Why do some rulers govern without meaningful elections, free media, or the rule of law — and why are so many of them so durable? This module introduces the comparative politics of authoritarian regimes: how dictatorships are organised, how they survive, and how they fall.
We examine the major varieties of authoritarian rule — personalist, single-party, military, monarchical, and hybrid or “electoral authoritarian” — and the core strategies autocrats use to stay in power: co-optation, repression, propaganda, elections without democracy, and managing rival elites. Cases are drawn from Russia, China, the Middle East, Latin America, and Africa.
The organising idea runs through every week: a dictator has two problems, not one — controlling the people who put him in power, and controlling everybody else. Nearly everything authoritarian regimes do (parties, parliaments, elections, propaganda, the secret police) is an answer to one of those two problems, and by the end of term you should be able to look at an unfamiliar regime and work out which one it is currently losing.

Learning outcomes
On successful completion of this module, you should be able to:

Distinguish between the major types of authoritarian regime and explain how they differ in their institutions and survival strategies.
Explain the central dilemmas autocrats face — the problems of power-sharing and of control — and the tools they use to manage them.
Evaluate competing theories of authoritarian durability, repression, co-optation, and regime breakdown.
Assess how elections, parties, propaganda, and information operate under authoritarian conditions.
Apply concepts and research from comparative politics to analyse contemporary authoritarian regimes and the global state of democracy.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
How the module works

Lectures
There are eleven lectures, one a week, Fridays 14:00–16:00, across teaching weeks 1–6 and 8–12. Reading week (teaching week 7) has no lecture.
Discussion happens inside the two-hour block: each session mixes presentation with argument, cases, and questions. Come having done the reading.
Attendance is not taken, but material is covered in the room that is not in the readings, and the slides are a prompt for what I say, not a transcript of it.
Slides are posted on the course website after each lecture.


Readings
There is no set textbook. Readings are journal articles and book chapters. Journal articles you find yourself, through the Library or Google Scholar — part of the training. Book chapters and anything else you cannot easily find are provided via Blackboard. Five books recur often enough that you will get to know them:

Milan Svolik, The Politics of Authoritarian Rule (Cambridge, 2012)
Barbara Geddes, Joseph Wright & Erica Frantz, How Dictatorships Work (Cambridge, 2018)
Steven Levitsky & Lucan Way, Competitive Authoritarianism (Cambridge, 2010)
Jennifer Gandhi, Political Institutions under Dictatorship (Cambridge, 2008)
Sergei Guriev & Daniel Treisman, Spin Dictators (Princeton, 2022)

Each week has required readings to complete before the lecture, plus recommended readings for going deeper. Some weeks also carry a short Bonus list — a blog post, an essay, a podcast episode, a film. Bonus items are not course material: not required, not examinable, and not sources for your written work. The list in the schedule below is indicative; Blackboard and the course website carry the current version.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Policies

Late work
All late work, unless excused in advance by me, is penalised at 5 marks per day or part thereof, up to a maximum of 20 marks. There are many good reasons a student cannot submit on time and I am happy to make reasonable accommodations, but not for requests made after the deadline or a few hours before it.
Requests go through your College Tutor, who contacts me. Extensions are not granted retrospectively except in exceptional medical circumstances, which require a medical certificate. Work is not accepted after it has been marked and returned to other students, or after the end of teaching term — in both cases the mark is 0. It is your responsibility to make sure your College Tutor knows the correct procedure.


Contacting me
Email me at noah.buckley@tcd.ie. Read this document first.
I will do my best to reply within two business days. Email is for logistics: extensions, difficulties, things only I can settle. For substantive questions about the material, come to office hours (by appointment) or raise it in lecture. I will not be able to fill you in on a lecture you missed.


Disability
Students with a disability liable to affect their ability to participate fully in this — or any — module are encouraged to register with the University’s Disability Service, which exists to make sure appropriate accommodations are in place.


Discussion in the room
The lecture is where the arguing happens. People in the room have different backgrounds and personal stakes in these questions — several of the regimes we study are somebody’s home country. Engage seriously with the arguments and generously with the people making them.


Keeping up with current events
Read the news! Any serious source you like, national or international. This is a module about the present tense as much as the past one. Half the value of it is having something concrete in your head when a concept turns up, and the other half is noticing that a concept explains something you read last week.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Academic integrity
Do not plagiarise. Academic dishonesty is a serious matter with serious consequences, up to and including no credit for the assignment, failure of the module, and expulsion. It is never permissible to submit work containing other people’s ideas without acknowledgment, and careless note-taking is not an excuse: put direct quotations in quotation marks, and reference paraphrases too. Trinity’s guidance is at libguides.tcd.ie/plagiarism, and if you have not already completed the Library’s Ready, Steady, Write tutorial, do that before your first submission. You must also submit only new work — not work submitted previously for another module.

Generative AI
These tools exist, you probably use them, and you will almost certainly use them in whatever you do after you get your college degree. But this module is not assessing whether you can obtain a competent paragraph about authoritarian politics from an LLM. It is assessing whether you can read an argument, find its weak point, and put your own case in your own words. So, in general: use these tools to help guide you and to help you fix your prose; do not use them to do your thinking or produce the prose.
What is permitted for each assessment is in that assessment’s sheet, in the vocabulary of the School of Social Sciences and Philosophy Assignment Submission Form — the same words you tick on the form. “Permitted” means you may do it and must tick the box. “Not permitted” means doing it is an academic integrity matter, whether or not you disclose it. The examination is in person and is not covered: nothing to declare, no form.
Trinity offers further resources in the Statement on Generative AI, the Library’s GenAI guide, and the College GenAI hub.


The Assignment Submission Form
Every piece of written work — response papers and the mid-term essay — must have the Assignment Submission Form as its first page. This is a department-wide rule. The form is on Blackboard in Word and PDF. Complete it in full, including the plagiarism declaration and the GenAI disclosure, ticking every category that applies to what you actually did. A submission without a completed form is not accepted — it is returned unmarked and treated as not submitted, accruing late penalties until you resubmit with one. The form does not count toward your word limit, and ticking a permitted box carries no penalty.
I reserve the right to modify this outline as necessary during term. The current version is always the one on the course website and Blackboard.

title: POU33201: Authoritarianism
text:
Schedule

Part I — Foundations

Teaching week 1 · Fri 18 September
What is authoritarianism? How much of the world is unfree, and the two questions the module returns to: how autocracies work, and why they last.
Required:

Erica Frantz. 2018. Authoritarianism: What Everyone Needs to Know. Oxford University Press. pp. 1–13.
Sergei Guriev and Daniel Treisman. 2019. “Informational Autocrats.” Journal of Economic Perspectives 33(4): 100–127.

Recommended:

Juan J. Linz. 2000. Totalitarian and Authoritarian Regimes. Lynne Rienner Publishers. Ch. 1.
Barbara Geddes, Joseph Wright and Erica Frantz. 2018. How Dictatorships Work. Cambridge University Press.
Robert A. Dahl. 1971. Polyarchy: Participation and Opposition. Yale University Press.
Juan J. Linz and Alfred Stepan. 1996. Problems of Democratic Transition and Consolidation: Southern Europe, South America, and Post-Communist Europe. Johns Hopkins University Press. Ch. 3.


Bonus:

Tom Pepinsky. 2017. “Everyday Authoritarianism is Boring and Tolerable.” Blog post.
Meduza. 17 September 2026. “Russia’s First Parliamentary Election Since the Full-Scale Invasion of Ukraine Begins Tomorrow, With Its Only Anti-War Party Barred and Genuine Competition All But Eliminated.” News.
The Moscow Times. 16 September 2026. “Russians Prepare for an Election With Less Choice Than Ever.” News.




Teaching week 2 · Fri 25 September
Varieties of autocracy. Personalist, single-party, military, monarchical and hybrid regimes, and why classifying them is hard.
Required:

Erica Frantz. 2018. Authoritarianism: What Everyone Needs to Know. Oxford University Press. Ch. 5.
Steven Levitsky and Lucan A. Way. 2002. “Elections Without Democracy: The Rise of Competitive Authoritarianism.” Journal of Democracy 13(2): 51–65.
Milan W. Svolik. 2012. The Politics of Authoritarian Rule. Cambridge University Press. Ch. 1 and 2 (pp. 1–45). This is dense and sometimes technical – focus on the main ideas

Recommended:

Jason Brownlee. 2007. “Hereditary Succession in Modern Autocracies.” World Politics 59(4): 595–628.
Beatriz Magaloni and Ruth Kricheli. 2010. “Political Order and One-Party Rule.” Annual Review of Political Science 13: 123–143.
Larry Diamond. 2002. “Elections Without Democracy: Thinking About Hybrid Regimes.” Journal of Democracy 13(2): 21–35.
Juan J. Linz. 2000. Totalitarian and Authoritarian Regimes. Lynne Rienner Publishers. Ch. 2.
David Collier and Steven Levitsky. 1997. “Democracy with Adjectives: Conceptual Innovation in Comparative Research.” World Politics 49(3): 430–451.
Victor Menaldo. 2012. “The Middle East and North Africa’s Resilient Monarchs.” The Journal of Politics 74(3): 707–722.
H. E. Chehabi and Juan J. Linz. 1998. Sultanistic Regimes. Johns Hopkins University Press. Ch. 1.




Part II — The dictator’s dilemmas

Teaching week 3 · Fri 2 October
How autocrats take and hold power. Ruling coalitions, elites, and why autocrats can’t simply trust one another.
Required:

Barbara Geddes, Joseph Wright and Erica Frantz. 2018. How Dictatorships Work. Cambridge University Press. Chs. 1–2.
Milan W. Svolik. 2012. The Politics of Authoritarian Rule. Cambridge University Press. Ch. 3 (pp. 53–63).

Recommended:

Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson. 2006. Economic Origins of Dictatorship and Democracy. Cambridge University Press. Introduction.
Georgy Egorov and Konstantin Sonin. 2011. “Dictators and Their Viziers: Endogenizing the Loyalty-Competence Trade-off.” Journal of the European Economic Association 9(5): 903–930.
Carles Boix and Milan W. Svolik. 2013. “The Foundations of Limited Authoritarian Government: Institutions, Commitment, and Power-Sharing in Dictatorships.” Journal of Politics 75(2): 300–316.
Gordon Tullock. 1987. Autocracy. Kluwer Academic Publishers.
Bruce Bueno de Mesquita and Alastair Smith. 2011. The Dictator’s Handbook: Why Bad Behavior Is Almost Always Good Politics. 1 ed. PublicAffairs.
Roger B. Myerson. 2008. “The Autocrat’s Credibility Problem and Foundations of the Constitutional State.” American Political Science Review 102(1): 125–139.



Teaching week 4 · Fri 9 October
The control problem: repression. Too much repression and too little are both dangerous — does it work, and when does it backfire?
Required:

Christian Davenport. 2007. “State Repression and Political Order.” Annual Review of Political Science 10(1): 1–23.
Ronald Wintrobe. 1998. The Political Economy of Dictatorship. Cambridge University Press. Selected pages TBA.
Milan W. Svolik. 2012. The Politics of Authoritarian Rule. Cambridge University Press. Ch. 5 (pp. 123–138).

Recommended:

Gary King, Jennifer Pan and Margaret E. Roberts. 2013. “How Censorship in China Allows Government Criticism but Silences Collective Expression.” American Political Science Review 107(2): 326–343.
Lisa Blaydes. 2018. State of Repression: Iraq under Saddam Hussein. Princeton University Press. Ch. 1.
Ronald Wintrobe. 1990. “The Tinpot and the Totalitarian: An Economic Theory of Dictatorship.” American Political Science Review 84(3): 849–872.
Mai Hassan, Daniel Mattingly and Elizabeth R. Nugent. 2022. “Political Control.” Annual Review of Political Science 25: 155–174.




Part III — Survival strategies

Teaching week 5 · Fri 16 October
Buying loyalty: parties, parliaments & patronage. Why dictatorships bother with parties and parliaments, and who’s worth buying — elites or masses.
Required:

Jennifer Gandhi and Adam Przeworski. 2007. “Authoritarian Institutions and the Survival of Autocrats.” Comparative Political Studies 40(11): 1279–1301.
Beatriz Magaloni. 2008. “Credible Power-Sharing and the Longevity of Authoritarian Rule.” Comparative Political Studies 41(4–5): 715–741.

Recommended:

Ellen Lust-Okar. 2006. “Elections Under Authoritarianism: Preliminary Lessons From Jordan.” Demokratizatsiya: The Journal of Post-Soviet Democratization 13(3): 1–17.
Milan W. Svolik. 2012. The Politics of Authoritarian Rule. Cambridge University Press. Ch. 6.
Lisa Blaydes. 2011. Elections and Distributive Politics in Mubarak’s Egypt. Cambridge University Press.
Adam Przeworski and Fernando Limongi. 1993. “Political Regimes and Economic Growth.” Journal of Economic Perspectives 7(3): 51–69.
Mancur Olson. 1993. “Dictatorship, Democracy, and Development.” American Political Science Review 87(3): 567–576.
Jennifer Gandhi. 2008. Political Institutions Under Dictatorship. Cambridge University Press.
Thomas B. Pepinsky. 2014. “The Institutional Turn in Comparative Authoritarianism.” British Journal of Political Science 44(3): 631–653.
Ora John Reuter. 2017. The Origins of Dominant Parties: Building Authoritarian Institutions in Post-Soviet Russia. Cambridge University Press.



Teaching week 6 · Fri 23 October
Elections without democracy. Why hold elections you might lose or have to rig, and what elections actually do for autocrats.
Required:

Andreas Schedler. 2002. “Elections Without Democracy: The Menu of Manipulation.” Journal of Democracy 13(2): 36–50.
Beatriz Magaloni. 2006. Voting for Autocracy. Cambridge University Press. Selected chapters TBA.

Recommended:

Carl Henrik Knutsen, Håvard Mokleiv Nygård and Tore Wig. 2017. “Autocratic Elections: Stabilizing Tool or Force for Change?” World Politics 69(1): 98–143.

Jennifer Gandhi and Ellen Lust-Okar. 2009. “Elections Under Authoritarianism.” Annual Review of Political Science 12: 403–422.
Andreas Schedler. 2013. The Politics of Uncertainty: Sustaining and Subverting Electoral Authoritarianism. Oxford University Press.

Reading week (teaching week 7) — w/c Monday 26 October. No lecture. Teaching resumes with teaching week 8 on Friday 6 November.


Teaching week 8 · Fri 6 November
Propaganda & censorship. Fear dictators against spin dictators, and why produce propaganda nobody believes.
Required:

Sergei Guriev and Daniel Treisman. 2022. Spin Dictators. Princeton University Press. Selected chapters TBA.
Haifeng Huang. 2015. “Propaganda as Signaling.” Comparative Politics 47(4): 419–444.

Recommended:

Gary King, Jennifer Pan and Margaret E. Roberts. 2013. “How Censorship in China Allows Government Criticism but Silences Collective Expression.” American Political Science Review 107(2): 326–343.
Hannah Arendt. 1951. The Origins of Totalitarianism. Harcourt Brace Jovanovich. Selected pages, on propaganda.
Václav Havel. 1985. “The Power of the Powerless.” In The Power of the Powerless: Citizens Against the State in Central-Eastern Europe, edited by John Keane. Routledge.
Arturas Rozenas and Denis Stukal. 2019. “How Autocrats Manipulate Economic News: Evidence from Russia’s State-Controlled Television.” The Journal of Politics 81(3): 982–996.
Georgy Egorov, Sergei Guriev and Konstantin Sonin. 2009. “Why Resource-Poor Dictators Allow Freer Media: A Theory and Evidence from Panel Data.” American Political Science Review 103(4): 645–668.



Teaching week 9 · Fri 13 November
Digital authoritarianism. What mass surveillance actually buys a regime, and how autocrats reach dissidents abroad.
Required:

Sebastian Hellmeier. 2016. “The Dictator’s Digital Toolkit: Explaining Variation in Internet Filtering in Authoritarian Regimes.” Politics & Policy 44(6): 1158–1191.
Xu Xu. 2021. “To Repress or to Co-opt? Authoritarian Control in the Age of Digital Surveillance.” American Journal of Political Science 65(2): 309–325.

Recommended:

Part IV — Threats & breakdown

Teaching week 10 · Fri 20 November
Coups & the military. The coup trap — the people who keep you in power can remove you — and the cost of coup-proofing.

Protest, revolution & breakdown. Preference falsification, why revolutions surprise everyone, and how autocracies actually end.

Part II: The Dictator’s Dilemmas


Teaching Week 3: How Autocrats Take and Hold Power (Friday 2 October 2026)
Topics: How dictatorships form, and why ruling elites can’t simply trust one another.
Required readings:

Barbara Geddes, Joseph Wright and Erica Frantz. 2018. How Dictatorships Work. Cambridge University Press. Chs. 1–2.
Milan W. Svolik. 2012. The Politics of Authoritarian Rule. Cambridge University Press. Ch. 3 (pp. 53–63).



Teaching Week 4: The Control Problem — Repression (Friday 9 October 2026)
Topics: The dictator’s dilemma — how much repression is enough, and when it backfires.
Required readings:

Christian Davenport. 2007. “State Repression and Political Order.” Annual Review of Political Science 10(1): 1–23.
Ronald Wintrobe. 1998. The Political Economy of Dictatorship. Cambridge University Press. Selected pages TBA.
Milan W. Svolik. 2012. The Politics of Authoritarian Rule. Cambridge University Press. Ch. 5 (pp. 123–138).



Part III: Survival Strategies


Teaching Week 5: Buying Loyalty — Parties, Parliaments & Patronage (Friday 16 October 2026)
Topics: Why dictatorships build parties and parliaments, and who they buy off to survive.
Required readings:

Jennifer Gandhi and Adam Przeworski. 2007. “Authoritarian Institutions and the Survival of Autocrats.” Comparative Political Studies 40(11): 1279–1301.
Beatriz Magaloni. 2008. “Credible Power-Sharing and the Longevity of Authoritarian Rule.” Comparative Political Studies 41(4–5): 715–741.



Teaching Week 6: Elections Without Democracy (Friday 23 October 2026)
Topics: Why autocrats hold elections they could just cancel, and what rigging actually buys them.
Required readings:

Andreas Schedler. 2002. “Elections Without Democracy: The Menu of Manipulation.” Journal of Democracy 13(2): 36–50.
Beatriz Magaloni. 2006. Voting for Autocracy. Cambridge University Press. Selected chapters TBA.



Teaching Week 7: Reading Week (w/c Monday 26 October 2026)
No lecture. Catch up on readings and work on your mid-term essay.
Mid-term essay due Sunday 1 November, 23:59, via Blackboard


Teaching Week 8: Propaganda & Censorship (Friday 6 November 2026)
Topics: Fear dictators versus spin dictators, and why propaganda nobody believes still works.
Required readings:

Sergei Guriev and Daniel Treisman. 2022. Spin Dictators. Princeton University Press. Selected chapters TBA.
Haifeng Huang. 2015. “Propaganda as Signaling.” Comparative Politics 47(4): 419–444.



Teaching Week 9: Digital Authoritarianism (Friday 13 November 2026)
Topics: What digital surveillance and censorship actually buy a regime, and what AI changes.
Required readings:

Sebastian Hellmeier. 2016. “The Dictator’s Digital Toolkit: Explaining Variation in Internet Filtering in Authoritarian Regimes.” Politics & Policy 44(6): 1158–1191.
Xu Xu. 2021. “To Repress or to Co-opt? Authoritarian Control in the Age of Digital Surveillance.” American Journal of Political Science 65(2): 309–325.



Part IV: Threats & Breakdown


Teaching Week 10: Coups & the Military (Friday 20 November 2026)
Topics: The coup trap — the people who keep a dictator in power are the ones who can remove him.
Required readings:

Sheena Chestnut Greitens. 2016. Dictators and Their Secret Police: Coercive Institutions and State Violence. Cambridge University Press. Ch. 1.
James T. Quinlivan. 1999. “Coup-Proofing: Its Practice and Consequences in the Middle East.” International Security 24(2): 131–165.
Barbara Geddes, Joseph Wright and Erica Frantz. 2018. How Dictatorships Work. Cambridge University Press. Military/coups chapter.



Teaching Week 11: Protest, Revolution & Breakdown (Friday 27 November 2026)
Topics: Why revolutions catch everyone by surprise, and how autocracies actually end.
Required readings:

Timur Kuran. 1991. “Now Out of Never: The Element of Surprise in the East European Revolution of 1989.” World Politics 44(1): 7–48.
Barbara Geddes, Joseph Wright and Erica Frantz. 2014. “Autocratic Breakdown and Regime Transitions: A New Data Set.” Perspectives on Politics 12(2): 313–331.



Teaching Week 12: Demise, Democratization & “Autocracy at Home?” (Friday 4 December 2026)
Topics: What comes after breakdown, and the global state of democracy the module leaves you with.
Required readings:

Steven Levitsky and Daniel Ziblatt. 2018. How Democracies Die. Crown. Selected chapters TBA.
Nancy Bermeo. 2016. “On Democratic Backsliding.” Journal of Democracy 27(1): 5–19.
Anna Lührmann and Staffan I. Lindberg. 2019. “A Third Wave of Autocratization Is Here: What Is New About It?” Democratization 26(7): 1095–1113.
